subtitle: From Molecules to Algorithms
entryAssumptions: Ability to follow a logical explanation

chapters.part: I · Representing and solving small problems
chapters.title: What does it mean to compute?
chapters.readerQuestion: Can the same rule work with counters and a calculator?
frames: Lay out three counters and add two
Move the counters one at a time
Read five counters and compare with a calculator display
chapters.mathBridge: Count tangible objects before writing 3 + 2 = 5; no variables or code syntax.
chapters.codeLab: Paper counter trace first; optional two-line Python add_two function imported into the printed listing. Generated exact cases and tests; no programming prerequisite.
chapters.exercise: Identify input and output; find an ambiguous instruction; explain why the material can change while the rule stays the same.

chapters.part: I · Representing and solving small problems
chapters.title: Symbols, information and representations
chapters.readerQuestion: How can a mark stand for something else?
frames: Match colored counters to written labels
Put the same labels in two different orders
Compare a collection with an ordered list
chapters.mathBridge: Show membership by placing cards inside a ring before set braces; use numbered positions before sequence notation.
chapters.codeLab: Encode a shopping list on paper and decode it using a supplied key.
chapters.exercise: Recognize a sequence versus a set; expose an ambiguous encoding; supply a decoding key.

chapters.part: I · Representing and solving small problems
chapters.title: Algorithms, decisions and remembered state
chapters.readerQuestion: How can a recipe choose and remember?
frames: Sort price cards using a yes/no question
Keep a running count in a labeled box
Repeat until no cards remain
chapters.mathBridge: Input/output pairs motivate a function; contrast with a relation permitting several outputs. Truth tables follow ordinary sentences.
chapters.codeLab: Write readable sorting pseudocode before Python; trace all state changes.
chapters.exercise: Complete a trace; test a boundary case; explain why an instruction must terminate.

chapters.part: I · Representing and solving small problems
chapters.title: Your first small Python programs
chapters.readerQuestion: How do instructions on paper become a runnable program?
frames: Read a plain-language instruction
Match it to one Python line
Run a tiny example and inspect a deliberately wrong result
chapters.mathBridge: Assignment is explained separately from mathematical equality; indexing begins with numbered cards.
chapters.codeLab: Teach installation or a browser interpreter, print, assignment, indexing, if, for, def and assertions in that order; no PyTorch.
chapters.exercise: Predict output before running; repair an index error; write a three-case test with supplied answers.

chapters.part: I · Representing and solving small problems
chapters.title: Cities, roads, graphs and paths
chapters.readerQuestion: How does a city map become a graph?
frames: Keep four city positions fixed and remove decoration
Replace cities with dots and roads with arrows
Trace a walk that repeats a city
Contrast a simple path and a closed cycle
chapters.mathBridge: Teach each visual term before G=(V,E); declare path means no repeated vertex, walk may repeat; count both edges and listed vertices.
chapters.codeLab: Trace routes with fingers, then represent adjacency as a dictionary using Chapter 4 as an optional implementation bridge.
chapters.exercise: Reject a backwards road; identify repeated vertices; compare path and cycle without requiring a named hard problem.

chapters.part: I · Representing and solving small problems
chapters.title: Search, counting and growing work
chapters.readerQuestion: Why can a tiny choice list grow so quickly?
frames: Arrange three cards in every order
Add a fourth card and count new positions
Compare ten, one hundred and one thousand items in a pair-checking table
chapters.mathBridge: Multiplication of choices precedes factorial; 100, 10000, 1000000 comparisons precede O(n²). Explain upper bound, not exact runtime.
chapters.codeLab: Enumerate small arrangements; compare a candidate generator with a separate checker.
chapters.exercise: Count a three-card case; find a checker bug; explain a small proof in words before notation.

chapters.part: II · DNA from zero
chapters.title: Atoms, molecules and different kinds of bonds
chapters.readerQuestion: What holds a molecule together?
frames: Group labeled atoms into a molecule
Highlight a connection within a molecule
Compare a weaker interaction between molecules
chapters.mathBridge: No formula needed: distinguish object counts, connections and charges before chemical symbols.
chapters.codeLab: Paper bond-key activity, not a molecular simulation.
chapters.exercise: Identify what each line style means; explain why base-pair marks must not look like backbone bonds.

chapters.part: II · DNA from zero
chapters.title: Solutions, amounts, temperature and change
chapters.readerQuestion: Why does the same molecule behave differently in different solutions?
frames: Keep volume fixed and change solute count
Keep amount fixed and change volume
Contrast a final balance with the speed of approaching it
chapters.mathBridge: Unit-labeled ratios precede concentration; introduce powers of ten and logarithm intuition before pH; energy landscapes are qualitative, not parameter predictions.
chapters.codeLab: Unit conversion and dilution worksheets; optional Python dimensional checks.
chapters.exercise: Distinguish rate from equilibrium; identify missing units; interpret a pH scale without an unsupported binding calculation.

chapters.part: II · DNA from zero
chapters.title: Cells, chromosomes, genes and genomes
chapters.readerQuestion: Where is DNA, and what is a genome?
frames: Show a labeled cell with scale warning
Zoom to chromosome and DNA
Mark a gene as a region, not an isolated bead
chapters.mathBridge: No equation; teach nested containment and distinguish a typical nucleated cell from bacteria and exceptions.
chapters.codeLab: Build a labeled containment map on paper.
chapters.exercise: Distinguish gene, chromosome and genome; explain why not every cell has a nucleus.

chapters.part: II · DNA from zero
chapters.title: From a nucleotide to a DNA strand
chapters.readerQuestion: What do the letters A, C, G and T leave out?
frames: Separate base, sugar and phosphate
Assemble one nucleotide
Join successive nucleotides along a backbone
Zoom out to a schematic double helix
chapters.mathBridge: Introduce chemical shorthand only after the object key; no atom-resolved geometry inferred from cartoons.
chapters.codeLab: Label a sequence-to-molecule correspondence; no physical inference from letters alone.
chapters.exercise: Distinguish base from nucleotide; locate the backbone; identify what a flattened drawing omits.

chapters.part: II · DNA from zero
chapters.title: Direction, pairing and reverse complement
chapters.readerQuestion: Why is a complement not yet a reverse complement?
frames: Number relevant sugar positions
Pair AACG with opposite-direction TTGC
Keep the partner fixed while reading from its other end
chapters.mathBridge: Show directions and paired letters before c(s) or RC(s); build round-trip reasoning from an asymmetric example.
chapters.codeLab: Plain Python character substitution, reversal and direction-labeled views, explained line by line.
chapters.exercise: Compute AGTC and ATAT partners; reject a wrong orientation; explain why a string test does not predict binding.

chapters.part: II · DNA from zero
chapters.title: Chance, encounters and repeated trials
chapters.readerQuestion: Why might a possible molecular encounter never be observed?
frames: Use a bag with one success card and nine misses
Replace the card and draw again
Compare both-miss with at-least-one-success cases
chapters.mathBridge: Explain sample space and fractions; 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81 precedes 1-(1-p)^M; flag independence as an assumption.
chapters.codeLab: Enumerate two-trial outcomes before a seeded simulation; explain seed as repeatable random-number setup.
chapters.exercise: Compute 0.19; contrast sampling with and without replacement; identify when the model is unjustified.

chapters.part: II · DNA from zero
chapters.title: From DNA to RNA and proteins
chapters.readerQuestion: What is copied, and what is translated?
frames: Keep a DNA template fixed while an RNA strand grows
Group RNA letters in threes
Build a schematic amino-acid chain
chapters.mathBridge: Teach alphabet and three-letter grouping before codon notation; introduce amino acids, transfer RNA and the ribosome through a labeled translation sequence. Enzyme mechanisms follow in Chapter 14.
chapters.codeLab: Translate a tiny supplied coding table by hand, then Python lookup; label the table deliberately incomplete.
chapters.exercise: Distinguish copying sequence from controlling a process; recognize that some RNAs are not translated.

chapters.part: II · DNA from zero
chapters.title: Enzymes and DNA replication in six frames
chapters.readerQuestion: Why are the two new strands made differently?
frames: Start with an intact duplex
Open a local region
Place primers
Extend from each primer's 3-prime end
Contrast continuous and discontinuous synthesis
Show two daughter duplexes
chapters.mathBridge: Teach new-strand and template directions before counting copies; distinguish an enzyme from a consumed nucleotide.
chapters.codeLab: Annotate fixed-position replication frames; no executable or wet-lab protocol required.
chapters.exercise: Locate the growing end; repair a reversed arrow; track parental versus newly synthesized strands.

chapters.part: III · Molecular operations and the laboratory
chapters.title: What a laboratory operation actually does
chapters.readerQuestion: What goes into an instrument, and what comes out?
frames: Transfer a labeled volume with a pipette
Separate sample components in a schematic centrifuge
Compare sample and control labels
chapters.mathBridge: Teach volume and instrument readings before uncertainty ranges; no hazardous or unsupervised recipe.
chapters.codeLab: Virtual sample ledger with units and controls; physical work requires supervised training.
chapters.exercise: Match instruments to purpose; spot a unit error; explain why an unlabeled tube invalidates interpretation.

chapters.part: III · Molecular operations and the laboratory
chapters.title: Hybridization as molecular recognition
chapters.readerQuestion: Why is compatible pairing not guaranteed binding?
frames: Compare matching and mismatching partners
Show reversible encounters in solution
Vary temperature while keeping sequence labels fixed
chapters.mathBridge: Energy difference and units before any equilibrium formula; empirical parameters must have provenance.
chapters.codeLab: Compare a logical match checker with a deliberately limited equilibrium model after parameters are sourced.
chapters.exercise: Separate compatibility, occupancy and reaction speed; identify unsupported numerical predictions.

chapters.part: III · Molecular operations and the laboratory
chapters.title: Cutting and joining strands
chapters.readerQuestion: How can cutting and joining act like instructions?
frames: Mark a recognition site without cutting
Cut at labeled positions
Align compatible ends
Join covalent backbones and show what remains unchanged
chapters.mathBridge: Track sequence positions before slice notation; orientation and chemical ends remain explicit.
chapters.codeLab: Plain Python cut-and-join model with precondition tests; explain its chemical omissions.
chapters.exercise: Predict fragments; reject incompatible orientation; distinguish association from covalent joining.

chapters.part: III · Molecular operations and the laboratory
chapters.title: Copying selected DNA with PCR
chapters.readerQuestion: How can a chosen DNA region become easier to detect?
frames: Separate paired strands
Attach primers
Extend new strands
Repeat a cycle and contrast ideal versus imperfect counts
chapters.mathBridge: Repeated doubling precedes 2^k; efficiency, plateau and unintended products are not hidden.
chapters.codeLab: Track ideal copy counts and then a supplied imperfect-copy scenario; not an executable bench protocol.
chapters.exercise: Identify primer direction; calculate two cycles; explain why real yield need not double.

chapters.part: III · Molecular operations and the laboratory
chapters.title: Separating molecules and retaining candidates
chapters.readerQuestion: How does a physical separation implement a selection rule?
frames: Load a labeled sample beside a reference
Move charged molecules through a gel
Compare bands
Retain a marked fraction with a documented selection rule
chapters.mathBridge: Teach reference size and relative migration first; no universal length-to-distance law.
chapters.codeLab: Simulate an ideal length filter and contrast with overlapping measurement bands.
chapters.exercise: Read a schematic gel; distinguish amount from length; explain what a blurry band cannot establish.

chapters.part: III · Molecular operations and the laboratory
chapters.title: Detecting and reading a result
chapters.readerQuestion: How does a molecular event become a reported answer?
frames: Order symbols into a conceptual synthesis request
Read a fluorescence signal with a control
Decode a schematic sequence trace
Mark an ambiguous result
chapters.mathBridge: Background and threshold before binary detection; do not convert no signal into proof of no candidate.
chapters.codeLab: Decode supplied traces with ambiguous bases preserved rather than guessed.
chapters.exercise: Explain synthesizer versus sequencer; reject an overconfident negative result; propose a control.

chapters.part: IV · Understanding the first DNA computer
chapters.title: Hamiltonian paths: a visual mini-course
chapters.readerQuestion: Can a route visit every city exactly once?
frames: Recall four cities and one-way roads
Try a route with a missing city
Try a repeated city
Keep a valid all-city route
Name Hamiltonian path only now
Close a cycle and compare
chapters.mathBridge: Only after valid/invalid pictures, write P=(v1,...,vn) and its conditions; explain each quantifier in words.
chapters.codeLab: Independent Python checker follows endpoint, legal-edge and unique-visit paper checks.
chapters.exercise: Recognition, route checking, implementation and reasoning ladder; fully work one valid and two invalid routes.

chapters.part: IV · Understanding the first DNA computer
chapters.title: Adleman's idea: encode a graph in DNA
chapters.readerQuestion: How can a molecule represent a city and a road?
frames: Place city symbols beside oriented DNA words
Align a road-encoding bridge
Join a possible route
Decode to the original cities
chapters.mathBridge: Define code length and overlap only after paired illustrations; distinguish teaching instance from the historical seven-vertex experiment.
chapters.codeLab: Encode and decode a tiny original graph; independently check adjacency.
chapters.exercise: Spot encoding ambiguity; trace one joined candidate; explain that a correct code does not guarantee physical generation.

chapters.part: IV · Understanding the first DNA computer
chapters.title: Generate, filter and read the candidates
chapters.readerQuestion: Why is one filter not enough?
frames: Generate several labeled candidate routes
Retain endpoints
Retain required length
Retain vertex coverage
Read and independently check survivors
chapters.mathBridge: Count retained candidates before set-filter notation; distinguish sample abundance from distinct strings.
chapters.codeLab: Rebuild the old token example only after paper filtering; separate generator, filter and oracle.
chapters.exercise: Keep a repeated-vertex counterexample until coverage; explain absent candidates versus missed detection.

chapters.part: IV · Understanding the first DNA computer
chapters.title: What the experiment proved, and what it did not
chapters.readerQuestion: Why is a small successful experiment not a shortcut around hard search?
frames: Separate a valid survivor from coverage of all possible answers
Place logical assumptions beside physical failure points
Compare time, molecules and readout
chapters.mathBridge: Plain reasoning precedes proposition and proof; explain the assumptions separately for checking survivors and generating every possible answer. Complexity-class terminology waits for the machine and reduction foundations in Chapter 25.
chapters.codeLab: Measure tiny enumerations; label counts as model counts, not laboratory yields or asymptotic empirical evidence.
chapters.exercise: Find a missing completeness premise; audit exponential material demand; state the bounded historical conclusion.

chapters.part: V · Building more molecular programs
chapters.title: Languages, machines and computational models
chapters.readerQuestion: What does it mean for different machines to solve the same kind of problem?
frames: Sort accepted and rejected symbol strings
Follow a turnstile state diagram
Add a read/write tape
Translate a small logical condition into a checking task
chapters.mathBridge: Teach Boolean variable, clause and satisfiability before SAT; accepted sets before formal-language notation. Explain decision tasks, polynomial-time checking and a concrete reduction before defining NP and NP-complete; distinguish nondeterminism from physical parallelism.
chapters.codeLab: Implement a two-state recognizer before a tiny tape-machine interpreter.
chapters.exercise: Trace acceptance; explain nondeterminism versus randomness; mark theorem assumptions and idealized unlimited storage.

chapters.part: V · Building more molecular programs
chapters.title: Strand, sticker and paired-strand models
chapters.readerQuestion: What changes when the allowed molecular instructions change?
frames: Mark a strand's occupied and empty sites
Execute one sticker operation
Compare a paired-tape reading head with a physical duplex
chapters.mathBridge: Operation tables precede model tuples; keep variants and their computational powers separate.
chapters.codeLab: Implement one named model variant with explicit allowed instructions.
chapters.exercise: Recognize a model operation; trace a program; reject a theorem transferred between variants.

chapters.part: V · Building more molecular programs
chapters.title: Splicing and rewriting strings
chapters.readerQuestion: Can cutting and joining describe a formal language?
frames: Mark two cut contexts
Exchange allowed suffixes
Generate a new string
Compare a rule-system derivation with a chemical cut
chapters.mathBridge: Concrete substitutions precede formal rewriting notation; alphabet, context and rule conditions stay visible.
chapters.codeLab: Plain Python one-step derivation and bounded search with independent hand cases.
chapters.exercise: Apply a rule; identify an illegal cut; distinguish formal closure from laboratory feasibility.

chapters.part: V · Building more molecular programs
chapters.title: Reaction networks and changing amounts
chapters.readerQuestion: How can amounts change step by step?
frames: Count two species in a container
Fire one permitted reaction
Subtract consumed and add produced objects
Compare many random histories
chapters.mathBridge: Old amount minus loss plus input precedes recurrence; stoichiometric counts and units precede rate equations; introduce derivative as instantaneous rate only if needed.
chapters.codeLab: Exact count simulator before a stochastic simulation; expose the assumptions and seed.
chapters.exercise: Compute two updates; check conservation; distinguish one random path from an average.

chapters.part: V · Building more molecular programs
chapters.title: Strand displacement in slow motion
chapters.readerQuestion: How can one strand release another without an enzyme?
frames: Show an intact gate and incoming strand
Bind a toehold
Advance branch migration in stable positions
Release the output
Contrast a leakage path
chapters.mathBridge: Teach domain labels before domain-level notation; rates require sourced parameters.
chapters.codeLab: Domain-level symbolic simulator, then compare against a published kinetic model when audited.
chapters.exercise: Track conserved strands; correct an orientation mistake; identify omitted side reactions.

chapters.part: V · Building more molecular programs
chapters.title: Digital and analog molecular circuits
chapters.readerQuestion: How can small reactions be connected into a larger computation?
frames: Solve a two-input logic question with cards
Replace one gate with molecular operations
Compose two gates
Contrast discrete decisions with continuously varying amounts
chapters.mathBridge: Truth table precedes Boolean expression; scaled concentration precedes analog formula; feedback sign is explained.
chapters.codeLab: Simulate truth-table behavior and a graded response separately, with interface contracts.
chapters.exercise: Check all inputs; identify signal depletion; explain why correct isolated gates need not compose reliably.

chapters.part: V · Building more molecular programs
chapters.title: Local assembly, tiles and DNA origami
chapters.readerQuestion: How can local attachments create a larger pattern?
frames: Match edge labels on two tiles
Grow a small pattern by local rules
Contrast tiles with a folded scaffold
Locate an address on the folded object
chapters.mathBridge: Coordinates follow grid pictures; no assumption that geometric assembly computes the same function as a circuit.
chapters.codeLab: Implement a bounded grid assembly model before inspecting a published origami design.
chapters.exercise: Find a forbidden attachment; distinguish shape from algorithm; state the physical scale boundary.

chapters.part: VI · From molecular systems to the next book
chapters.title: Genes, regulation, development and evolution
chapters.readerQuestion: How can the same DNA support different cellular behavior?
frames: Keep DNA fixed while a control signal changes expression
Compare two cell states
Show a heritable sequence change
Track variation and selection across generations
chapters.mathBridge: Separate within-cell state change from inherited population change; simple frequency counts precede population notation.
chapters.codeLab: Toy control and selection ledgers with explicit biological omissions; no claim of a living simulation.
chapters.exercise: Identify regulatory control versus sequence transfer; distinguish adaptation, mutation and development.

chapters.part: VI · From molecular systems to the next book
chapters.title: DNA storage, codes and recovery
chapters.readerQuestion: How can a message survive a damaged molecular copy?
frames: Map a short message to symbols
Insert one substitution or missing symbol
Use redundancy to recover or flag ambiguity
Select a requested block
chapters.mathBridge: Teach bit choices and code distance before coding bounds; probability and logarithm recall precede entropy, without claiming one universal capacity.
chapters.codeLab: Plain Python encode, corrupt, decode, and test undecodable cases.
chapters.exercise: Recover a toy message; measure overhead; distinguish storage from active molecular computation.

chapters.part: VI · From molecular systems to the next book
chapters.title: Many numbers at once: vectors, matrices and DNA data
chapters.readerQuestion: Why do sequence-analysis programs use arrays of numbers?
frames: Turn three sequence features into a row of numbers
Stack several rows into a table
Combine two feature rows with weights
Contrast software analyzing DNA with molecules computing
chapters.mathBridge: Ordered measurements precede vector notation; row-column weighted sums precede matrix products and dimensions.
chapters.codeLab: Plain Python vector sums and matrix multiplication on tiny examples; trained sequence models are only a destination, taught in Book II.
chapters.exercise: Check dimensions; compute a two-row result; explain the two meanings of DNA computation.

chapters.part: VI · From molecular systems to the next book
chapters.title: Resources, energy, reliability and design tools
chapters.readerQuestion: What must be counted before calling a design efficient?
frames: Give time, sample volume and measurement separate meters
Trace an error through two operations
Compare a model forecast with a supplied observation
Mark an unmeasured quantity as unknown
chapters.mathBridge: Attach units to every quantity before a cost tuple; no free-energy-to-computer-energy shortcut.
chapters.codeLab: Reproducible small model configuration and results ledger; tool versions and parameters are explicit.
chapters.exercise: Reconcile units; design a control; distinguish software tests from physical validation.

chapters.part: VI · From molecular systems to the next book
chapters.title: A measured frontier and the bridge to Evolutor
chapters.readerQuestion: What can you now build, explain and still not claim?
frames: Trace a small problem through representation, operation and readout
Place a conventional alternative alongside it
Mark what evidence is missing
Connect achieved learning outcomes to Book II entry checks
chapters.mathBridge: No new advanced formula; reconstruct earlier tools in a bounded capstone.
chapters.codeLab: Choose one simulation capstone, reproduce supplied results and record failures; no frontier performance claims without renewed sources.
chapters.exercise: Explain a mechanism, implement its checker, critique evidence and complete the Book II readiness tasks.
